name: Rear Naked Choke from Harness
summary: The Rear Naked Choke from Harness is a blood choke finished from back control, threading the seatbelt's over-the-shoulder arm under the opponent's chin to compress both carotid arteries and force the tap.
description: Master the Rear Naked Choke from Harness in BJJ. Complete guide to grip transitions, choking mechanics, defense strategies, and safety protocols.
overview:
Built on the seatbelt grip already established in the harness, this attack represents the natural offensive culmination of that control system. From the harness position, the attacker has already established the over-under arm configuration that serves as the foundation for the choking mechanics. The transition from harness grip to rear naked choke involves systematically advancing the choking arm from its controlling position across the opponent's chest to underneath the chin, where it compresses the carotid arteries bilaterally.

What distinguishes this entry specifically is the pre-existing structural control. Unlike attacks from scramble positions where the attacker must simultaneously establish control and threaten the neck, the harness provides a stable platform from which to methodically work past hand-fighting defenses. The underhook arm maintains postural control and prevents the rotation needed to escape, while the choking arm progressively advances toward the neck.

Strategically, this creates a cascading dilemma system. The opponent must commit both hands to defending the choking arm, preventing them from removing hooks or creating escape angles. If they release grip control to fight hooks or create space, the choking arm advances. This tension between positional defense and submission defense makes the harness-based RNC the cornerstone of every modern back attack system.

injury_risks.injury: Loss of consciousness from bilateral carotid compression
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate to 30 seconds with proper release

injury_risks.injury: Trachea damage from improper forearm placement on windpipe
Cervical spine strain from excessive cranking or twisting
Carotid artery dissection from excessive or rapid force
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate medical attention required, weeks to months

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum squeeze in training. Never snap or jerk the choke. Partner should have full awareness of pressure building before the choke becomes tight.
tap_signals: Verbal tap (say 'tap' or any verbal sound indicating submission)
Physical hand tap on opponent's body, arm, or mat (multiple taps)
Physical foot tap on mat when hands are trapped
Going limp or loss of consciousness requires immediate release
Any distress signal, unusual gurgling, or panicked movement
release_protocol: Immediately release choking arm upon any tap signal
Remove hooks and disengage body contact
Gently guide partner to side-lying recovery position
Monitor consciousness and breathing for 30 seconds minimum
If partner lost consciousness, keep them lying down with legs slightly elevated until fully alert
Never allow an unconscious partner to sit up or stand immediately
training_restrictions: Never use competition speed or intensity when drilling the choke
Never apply pressure to the trachea or windpipe - blade of wrist targets carotids only
Always ensure partner has clear tap access with at least one hand
Stop immediately if partner makes any distress sound or appears to panic
Never hold a choke past the tap for any reason, regardless of competition preparation
Beginners must practice with extremely slow, controlled progression only

variations_and_setups.description: The classic RNC where the choking arm slides under the chin, the free hand grabs the bicep of the choking arm, and the hand of the choking arm cups behind the opponent's head. Squeeze is generated by expanding the chest and pulling the elbows together.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Default finishing method when you can get the choking arm fully under the chin and lock the figure-four configuration without interference.

variations_and_setups.description: When the figure-four cannot be locked, the choking arm goes under the chin and the free hand pushes the back of the opponent's head forward into the choking forearm. Effective when the opponent is defending the lock hand from connecting to the bicep.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the opponent successfully prevents the figure-four lock by trapping or blocking the support hand from reaching the choking arm's bicep.

variations_and_setups.description: Both hands clasp together palm-to-palm with the choking forearm under the chin. The squeeze comes from pulling both hands toward the chest while expanding the ribcage. Less mechanically efficient than figure-four but faster to lock.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When speed of application matters more than mechanical perfection, particularly during scrambles or when the opponent is actively fighting the grip transition.

attacker.name: from Harness Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to execute the Rear Naked Choke from Harness. Step-by-step guide covering grip transitions, finishing mechanics, and responses to common defensive counters.
attacker.overview: Executing the Rear Naked Choke from Harness requires patience and systematic grip advancement. The primary challenge is transitioning from the controlling seatbelt configuration to the figure-four choking position while the opponent actively defends with two-on-one grip control, chin tucking, and shoulder shrugging. Success depends on creating dilemmas that force the opponent to choose between defending the choke and maintaining positional integrity, then capitalizing on the resulting openings with decisive arm placement and proper squeeze mechanics. The harness provides the ideal launching platform because the choking arm is already positioned over the shoulder, requiring only forward advancement rather than a full arm insertion from scratch.
key_principles: Maintain chest-to-back connection throughout the entire choke transition to prevent the opponent from creating the space needed to turn or escape
Advance the choking arm in small increments using elbow walking rather than attempting one large movement that the opponent can anticipate and block
Use the underhook arm to control the opponent's posture and prevent them from turning into you while the choking arm advances toward the neck
Create grip-breaking dilemmas by threatening the arm advancement from multiple angles so the opponent cannot establish a static two-on-one defense
Apply the squeeze through chest expansion and structural mechanics rather than relying on arm strength alone, which fatigues rapidly
Keep hooks active and engaged to prevent the opponent from using hip escapes or turns as an alternative to hand-fighting the choking arm
setup_requirements: Harness grip fully established with one arm over the opponent's shoulder (choking arm) and one arm under the opposite armpit, hands connected at the chest or sternum
At least one hook inserted with the instep controlling the opponent's inner thigh to prevent hip rotation and turning escapes
Chest-to-back connection maintained with forward pressure distributed through the core, not solely through grip tension
Head positioned safely to the side of the opponent's head, typically on the choking arm side, to avoid backward head pressure and maintain structural alignment
Opponent's defensive posture assessed to identify whether they are protecting the neck with hands high or fighting hooks with hands low

execution_steps.action: Confirm harness control and assess defensive posture
execution_steps.description: Before initiating the choke transition, verify that your seatbelt grip is tight with hands clasped high on the chest, at least one hook is secure, and your chest is pressed firmly against the opponent's back. Assess whether the opponent's hands are defending the neck or fighting your hooks, as this determines your initial advancement strategy.

execution_steps.action: Begin choking arm advancement with elbow walking
execution_steps.description: Start sliding the choking arm (the over-the-shoulder arm) from its position on the chest toward the opponent's neck. Use small elbow-walking movements rather than one large pull. Release the grip connection briefly if needed, using the underhook arm to maintain control while the choking hand advances one to two inches at a time toward the jawline.

The opponent will likely grab your choking wrist with both hands. Counter by using your free hand to peel their top grip finger by finger, or swim your underhook hand over their defending arm to strip grips. Alternatively, use a push-pull motion where you push their defending elbow away with your free hand while simultaneously advancing the choking arm forward. Create a dilemma by threatening an armbar if they commit both hands too aggressively.

execution_steps.action: Clear the chin barrier and slide the forearm under
execution_steps.description: Once grip control is established on the wrist defense, work the blade of your wrist along the jawline and under the chin. If the opponent tucks their chin hard, use your free hand to cup their forehead and tilt the head back slightly, or walk your choking arm across the face from ear to chin. The forearm should slide under the chin with the blade of the wrist centered on the throat, angled so the radius bone contacts the carotid arteries rather than the trachea.

Once the choking forearm is under the chin, immediately grab your own bicep with the choking hand while your free hand cups behind the opponent's head or grabs the crown. Pull your elbows together to close any remaining space. The crook of the choking elbow should be centered under the chin with the forearm and bicep creating bilateral pressure on both carotid arteries simultaneously. Ensure no pressure is on the trachea.

execution_steps.action: Apply the squeeze with proper body mechanics
execution_steps.description: Generate choking pressure by expanding your chest forward while pulling your elbows back and together. Think of squeezing your shoulder blades together behind the opponent's head. Use your hooks to prevent any last-second escape by pulling your heels into their thighs. The squeeze should be steady and progressive, not a sudden jerk. Your chest expansion creates the primary compression force while your arms maintain the structural frame around the neck.

execution_steps.action: Adjust angle and maintain pressure until tap
execution_steps.description: If the initial squeeze does not produce a tap, micro-adjust by angling your body slightly to one side to increase unilateral carotid pressure. Pull the opponent's body tighter against yours by engaging your hooks and arching your back slightly. Monitor for tap signals constantly. If the opponent's defense creates space in the figure-four, re-tighten by pulling elbows closer together and re-expanding the chest. Release immediately upon any tap signal.

common_counters.counter: Two-on-one grip control on the choking arm wrist, preventing advancement toward the neck
common_counters.your_response: Use your free hand to strip their top grip finger by finger while maintaining forward pressure on the choking arm. Alternatively, threaten an armbar on the defending arm to force them to release, or swim your underhook hand over their defending arm to break the grip structure.

common_counters.counter: Deep chin tuck with shoulder elevation creating a barrier to forearm entry under the chin
common_counters.your_response: Use your free hand to cup the forehead and tilt the head back, or walk the choking arm across the face from ear to chin. If chin remains tucked, apply the choke over the chin - the jaw acts as a lever that creates significant discomfort and often forces the opponent to lift their chin.

common_counters.counter: Turning the body toward the choking arm side and hip escaping to recover guard
common_counters.your_response: Follow the turn by adjusting your hooks and maintaining chest contact. Use the underhook arm to block their hip rotation and pull them back to center. If they commit fully to the turn, transition to a mounted triangle or crucifix position rather than fighting the rotation.

common_counters.counter: Stripping hooks while defending the neck to create escape mobility
common_counters.your_response: If opponent removes a hand from choking arm defense to fight hooks, immediately advance the choking arm toward the neck. The hook removal creates a momentary opening where only one hand defends the choke. Capitalize on this by accelerating the arm insertion before they can return both hands to the defense.

common_errors.error: Placing the forearm across the trachea instead of positioning the blade of the wrist against the carotid arteries
common_errors.consequence: Creates a painful but ineffective air choke that damages the windpipe and causes unnecessary injury without producing efficient blood flow restriction to the brain
common_errors.correction: Position the blade of the wrist (radius bone) directly against one carotid artery while the bicep compresses the other. The crook of the elbow should be centered under the chin with no bone contact on the trachea.

common_errors.error: Rushing the choke by releasing all control to grab the neck in one explosive movement
common_errors.consequence: Gives the opponent a clear window to strip the grip, turn into guard, or escape the back position entirely, losing a dominant position for a low-percentage scramble
common_errors.correction: Advance the choking arm in small increments using elbow walking while maintaining the underhook for postural control. Never sacrifice positional control for a rushed submission attempt.

common_errors.error: Releasing the underhook arm before the figure-four is fully locked to grab behind the head prematurely
common_errors.consequence: Loses the postural control that prevents the opponent from turning, allowing them to rotate their body and escape to guard or turtle before the choke is completed
common_errors.correction: Keep the underhook arm engaged for postural control until the choking arm is fully under the chin. Only release the underhook to complete the figure-four lock when the choking position is secured.

common_errors.error: Squeezing exclusively with arm muscles instead of using chest expansion and skeletal mechanics
common_errors.consequence: Causes rapid forearm fatigue, reduces squeeze power over time, and produces an inconsistent pressure that the opponent can outlast through pain tolerance
common_errors.correction: Generate primary choking pressure by expanding the chest and pulling shoulder blades together. Arms maintain the structural frame while the torso provides the compression force.

common_errors.error: Failing to address the chin tuck and repeatedly trying to force the arm under a locked jaw
common_errors.consequence: Wastes energy on a blocked entry point and telegraphs the attack, allowing the opponent to strengthen their defensive posture and potentially strip grips during the struggle
common_errors.correction: If the chin is locked down, redirect by choking over the chin using the jaw as a lever, tilting the head with the free hand, or walking the forearm across the face from ear to chin to bypass the barrier.

common_errors.error: Allowing the head to drift in front of the opponent's shoulder where they can create backward pressure
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can drive their head backward into your face, creating pain and forcing positional adjustments that compromise your choking mechanics and chest connection
common_errors.correction: Keep your head positioned to the choking arm side, tucked behind the opponent's shoulder or ear. Maintain head pressure against the side of their head to control their posture.

training_progressions.focus: Developing the motor pattern for transitioning from harness grip to figure-four RNC position
training_progressions.description: Practice the arm advancement sequence on a non-resisting partner. Focus on elbow walking, proper forearm placement under the chin, and locking the figure-four configuration. Repeat 20-30 times per side. Partner provides feedback on forearm placement relative to the trachea.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 2: Hand Fighting and Grip Breaking
training_progressions.focus: Learning to defeat common grip defenses while maintaining positional control
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes two-on-one defense on choking arm at 50% resistance. Practice grip stripping, swim moves, and push-pull grip breaks while keeping chest contact and hooks engaged. Gradually increase resistance over rounds. Add chin-tuck defense variations.

training_progressions.focus: Applying proper squeeze mechanics against progressively increasing defensive intensity
training_progressions.description: Start with the choking arm already under the chin and practice locking the figure-four and applying the squeeze at controlled intensity. Partner defends by fighting the lock hand and turning. Focus on chest expansion mechanics, shoulder blade squeeze, and hook engagement during the finish.

training_progressions.focus: Integrating the complete sequence from harness control through finish under live conditions
training_progressions.description: Positional sparring starting from established harness. Attacker works the complete sequence: grip advancement, defeating hand defense, chin clearing, locking, and finishing. Defender uses full resistance. Reset if back is lost. Track success rates and identify patterns in failed attempts for targeted improvement.

training_progressions.focus: Applying the choke under fatigue and time pressure simulating competition conditions
training_progressions.description: After 3-4 minutes of hard sparring, partner gives up the back intentionally. Practice executing the full RNC sequence while fatigued with competition-level resistance. Emphasize efficiency over power and pattern recognition for defensive tendencies. Include referee awareness and scoring considerations.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Rear Naked Choke from Harness primarily target?
flashcards.answer: The RNC targets both carotid arteries simultaneously using bilateral compression. The blade of the wrist (radius bone) compresses one carotid artery while the bicep of the choking arm compresses the other. This restricts blood flow to the brain, causing unconsciousness within 6-10 seconds of a properly applied choke. The trachea should not be compressed - the crook of the elbow is centered under the chin to create a pocket that protects the windpipe.

flashcards.question: Your opponent has a strong two-on-one grip on your choking arm wrist preventing any advancement - what grip-breaking strategy do you employ?
flashcards.answer: Use your free hand to peel their top grip starting with the pinky finger and peeling outward. Alternatively, swim your underhook hand over their defending forearm to strip their grip from above. A third option is the push-pull method where you push their defending elbow away with your free hand while simultaneously pulling the choking arm forward. If grip fighting stalls, threaten an armbar on their extended defending arm to create a choke-versus-armbar dilemma that forces them to release.

flashcards.question: What is the correct forearm placement to ensure a blood choke rather than an air choke?
flashcards.answer: The blade of the wrist (the bony edge of the radius) should contact one carotid artery while the bicep contacts the other. The crook of the elbow must be centered directly under the chin, creating a V-shaped pocket around the trachea that avoids windpipe compression. If you feel your forearm bone pressing against the front of the throat, you are on the trachea and must adjust laterally. The forearm should angle slightly so the radius targets the side of the neck, not the front.

flashcards.question: Your opponent tucks their chin tightly to their chest and you cannot slide the forearm under - how do you clear this barrier?
flashcards.answer: Three primary methods exist. First, use your free hand to cup the forehead and gently tilt the head backward to create space under the chin. Second, walk the choking forearm across the face from ear to chin, using the jawline as a ramp to slide underneath. Third, apply the choke over the chin - the jawbone acts as a painful lever that pressures the opponent into lifting their chin voluntarily. Avoid cranking the neck sideways, which risks cervical spine injury.

flashcards.question: What control elements must be established before initiating the choke transition from harness?
flashcards.answer: Five elements must be confirmed: tight seatbelt grip with hands clasped high on the chest near the collarbone, at least one hook inserted with instep controlling the inner thigh, chest pressed firmly against the opponent's back with forward pressure through the core, head positioned safely to the choking arm side behind the opponent's ear, and assessment of the opponent's hand positioning to determine whether they are defending the neck or fighting hooks.

flashcards.question: You have the choking arm under the chin but cannot lock the figure-four because the opponent is blocking your support hand - what finishing alternative exists?
flashcards.answer: Apply the short choke variation by using your free hand to push the back of the opponent's head forward into the choking forearm rather than locking a figure-four. Alternatively, use a palm-to-palm grip with the choking arm under the chin and both hands clasped together, squeezing by pulling toward your chest while expanding. Both alternatives sacrifice mechanical efficiency but can produce a tap when the standard figure-four is unavailable due to active hand defense.

flashcards.question: What is the proper application speed for the Rear Naked Choke in training and what are the risks of applying it too quickly?
flashcards.answer: Apply the squeeze slowly and progressively over 3-5 seconds minimum in training. Never snap or jerk the choke tight. Rapid application risks carotid artery injury, trachea damage if alignment is imperfect, and cervical spine strain from sudden force. The partner must have full awareness of building pressure to respond with a timely tap. In training, treat every choke as if the partner might not feel it immediately and always prioritize their safety over the finish.

flashcards.question: How should you immediately respond when your partner taps to the Rear Naked Choke?
flashcards.answer: Release the choking arm instantly upon any tap signal, including verbal taps, physical hand or foot taps, and any distress sounds. Remove hooks and disengage body contact. Guide the partner to a side-lying position and monitor their consciousness and breathing for at least 30 seconds. If the partner lost consciousness, keep them lying down with legs slightly elevated until they are fully alert and oriented. Never allow an unconscious partner to stand immediately.

flashcards.question: Your opponent begins turning their body toward your choking arm side while you have the arm partially advanced - how do you adjust?
flashcards.answer: Follow the turn by adjusting your hook position and maintaining chest-to-back contact. Use the underhook arm to block their hip rotation by pulling their far hip toward you. Drive your top hook deeper to prevent further rotation. If they commit fully to the turn, capitalize by advancing the choking arm during the movement since their defensive hands may shift to assist the turn. Alternatively, transition to mounted triangle or crucifix if the turn exposes their arm.

flashcards.question: What distinguishes the point of no escape in the RNC finishing sequence?
flashcards.answer: The point of no escape occurs when the figure-four lock is fully secured with the choking forearm under the chin, the free hand grabbing the bicep, and the lock hand behind the head. Once all three connection points are established and the elbows begin closing together, the bilateral carotid compression makes escape virtually impossible through hand fighting alone. Before this point, the opponent can still strip grips or create space. After the lock, only a dramatic positional escape like a forward roll has any chance of success.

defender.name: from Harness Defender
defender.description: Defend against the Rear Naked Choke from Harness. Learn recognition cues, hand fighting priorities, escape sequences, and critical survival strategies.
defender.overview: Defending the Rear Naked Choke from Harness demands constant vigilance and disciplined hand fighting. The primary objective is preventing the choking arm from reaching the neck by maintaining two-on-one control on the attacking wrist while simultaneously working to create angles and remove hooks. Understanding the attacker's grip progression allows the defender to anticipate each advancement stage before the choke becomes locked and the window for defense closes permanently. Survival in this position requires calm systematic defense rather than explosive panicked movements, which burn energy and create openings for the choke.
key_principles: Immediately establish two-on-one grip control on the choking arm wrist before it advances past the collarbone toward the neck
Keep the chin tucked tight to the chest and elevate the shoulder on the choking arm side to create a physical barrier against forearm entry
Never release control of the choking arm to fight hooks - the choke is the primary threat and hooks without a tight grip are far less dangerous
Turn toward the underhook side when attempting escapes to disrupt the attacker's structural alignment and create the most effective escape angle
Maintain calm and controlled breathing to prevent panic, conserve energy, and make clear tactical decisions under pressure
Address defensive priorities in sequence: control choking arm first, protect neck second, manage hooks third, then escape
recognition_cues: Opponent's over-the-shoulder arm begins sliding from its position on your chest toward your neck and jawline in small incremental advances
Opponent releases the harness grip lock to free the choking hand for advancement, creating a brief moment where their hands separate
Increased forward pressure through the chest and a head position change as the opponent shifts weight to support the choking arm transition
Opponent's free hand begins stripping your grip on the choking arm wrist, peeling fingers or swimming over your forearm
Opponent adjusts hook depth or body angle to optimize leverage for the arm advancement, often arching slightly or shifting hips

defensive_options.action: Two-on-one grip control on the choking arm wrist with both hands pulling it down toward your chest
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately upon recognizing the harness is established and the choking arm is positioned over your shoulder - this is the primary preventive defense
defensive_options.if_successful: Choking arm is neutralized at the chest level, preventing advancement toward the neck and buying time for positional escapes
defensive_options.risk: Both hands committed to choking arm defense leaves hooks uncontested, allowing opponent to establish deeper positional control

defensive_options.action: Chin tuck with shoulder elevation on the choking side creating a physical barrier to forearm entry
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the choking arm has advanced past the chest and is approaching the jawline - this is the secondary defensive layer
defensive_options.if_successful: Creates a physical wedge between the forearm and the neck that the attacker must work around, buying additional time for grip recovery
defensive_options.risk: Chin tuck alone is not sufficient defense - opponent can choke over the chin or walk the forearm around the jaw with sufficient patience

defensive_options.action: Turn toward the underhook side with hip escape to recover guard position
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you have successfully controlled the choking arm and created space from hooks, or when the position has become untenable and you need a dramatic positional change
defensive_options.if_successful: Escape to closed guard eliminates the back exposure and resets to a neutral guard position where the choke threat is removed
defensive_options.risk: If the turn is attempted without first neutralizing the choking arm, the rotation can accelerate the arm's path under the chin and result in an immediate choke

defensive_options.action: Strip one hook and hip escape to create angle before turning to face the opponent
defensive_options.when_to_use: When choking arm is controlled and you need to reduce the opponent's lower body control before completing the escape sequence
defensive_options.if_successful: Removing a hook significantly reduces the opponent's ability to maintain back control and makes the full turn to guard achievable
defensive_options.risk: Releasing one hand from choking arm control to fight hooks creates a brief window where the choke can advance

escape_paths: Control choking arm with two-on-one, turn toward underhook side, hip escape to create angle, strip hooks, and recover to closed guard facing the opponent
Strip grips and hooks systematically, transition to turtle position by getting to all fours, then work to standing or guard recovery from turtle

favorable_outcomes.how: Successfully control the choking arm, strip at least one hook, turn toward the underhook side with a hip escape to create enough angle to rotate fully and face the opponent, recovering into closed guard where the back exposure and choke threat are eliminated

common_errors.error: Reaching backward to grab the opponent's head or body without first controlling the choking arm
common_errors.consequence: Completely exposes the neck and allows the opponent to slide the choking arm under an undefended chin for an immediate rear naked choke finish
common_errors.correction: Always prioritize two-on-one control on the choking arm before any other defensive action. The neck is the primary target and must be defended first.

common_errors.error: Panicking and making explosive uncontrolled movements to escape
common_errors.consequence: Burns energy rapidly, creates openings as defensive grips slip during thrashing, and often results in worse positioning or an accelerated choke setup
common_errors.correction: Stay calm, breathe steadily through the nose, and work through defensive priorities systematically. Address one problem at a time: control arm, protect neck, manage hooks, then escape.

common_errors.error: Releasing choking arm control to fight hooks before the choke threat is neutralized
common_errors.consequence: Allows the choking arm to advance unchecked toward the neck while gaining only marginal benefit from hook removal, since hooks without a tight grip are manageable
common_errors.correction: Maintain two-on-one on the choking arm until it is firmly controlled at chest level. Only release one hand to fight hooks when you are confident the choking arm cannot advance during the grip transition.

common_errors.error: Turning away from the underhook side during escape attempts
common_errors.consequence: Plays directly into the opponent's harness control structure, tightening the choke angle and making the seatbelt more effective rather than disrupting it
common_errors.correction: Always turn toward the underhook side. This disrupts the opponent's structural alignment, creates the optimal escape angle, and makes the harness grip less effective.

common_errors.error: Tapping too late after the choke is fully locked and blood flow is restricted
common_errors.consequence: Risks loss of consciousness, potential carotid artery injury, and cervical spine damage from holding out against a fully applied blood choke
common_errors.correction: Tap early and tap clearly. Once the figure-four is locked and the squeeze begins, recognize that the choke is mechanically secured and continuing to defend risks injury. There is no shame in acknowledging a successfully applied submission.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that the Rear Naked Choke from Harness is being initiated?
flashcards.answer: Key recognition cues include the opponent's over-the-shoulder arm beginning to slide from the chest toward the jawline, the opponent releasing their harness grip lock to free the choking hand, increased chest pressure and head positioning changes, and the opponent's free hand starting to strip your defensive grips on the choking wrist. Early recognition before the arm passes the collarbone is critical for successful defense.

flashcards.question: What is the correct priority sequence when defending the Rear Naked Choke from Harness?
flashcards.answer: The priority sequence is: first, establish two-on-one grip control on the choking arm to prevent it from reaching the neck. Second, protect the neck with chin tuck and shoulder elevation as a secondary barrier. Third, prevent or remove hooks to restore lower body mobility. Fourth, create angles through hip escape and turn toward the underhook side to disrupt the attacker's alignment. Fifth, complete the escape to guard or turtle. Never skip steps or address a lower priority before securing the higher ones.

flashcards.question: When should you tap to the Rear Naked Choke and what is the safest way to signal submission?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately once the figure-four lock is secured and the squeeze begins producing bilateral carotid pressure. Do not wait for vision changes or lightheadedness. Signal with a clear physical tap on the opponent's arm or body using multiple rapid taps, or verbally say 'tap' loudly. If your hands are trapped, use foot taps on the mat. A properly locked RNC produces unconsciousness within 6-10 seconds, so the window for tapping is narrow once the choke is fully applied.

flashcards.question: What escape options remain if the choking arm is already partially under your chin?
flashcards.answer: Immediately grab the choking wrist with both hands and pull it below your chin while simultaneously tucking your chin hard to trap the forearm against your jawline. Turn your chin toward the inside of the choking elbow to create space and reduce compression. If the arm continues advancing, fight the lock hand by preventing it from connecting to the bicep. As a last resort, attempt an explosive turn toward the underhook side to create enough rotational force to dislodge the choking arm before the figure-four locks.

flashcards.question: How does proper body positioning reduce the effectiveness of the attacker's choke attempt?
flashcards.answer: Maintaining a slightly rounded posture with shoulders curled forward reduces the space available for the choking arm to slide under the chin. Turning slightly toward the underhook side disrupts the attacker's bilateral alignment and makes the seatbelt less structurally effective. Keeping hips low and heavy on the mat reduces the attacker's leverage from their hooks. Elevating the shoulder on the choking side creates a physical shelf that blocks forearm entry. These positioning details compound to make the choke significantly harder to execute.

training_progressions.focus: Developing the instinct to immediately secure the choking arm upon recognizing back control
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes harness grip and slowly begins advancing the choking arm. Defender practices recognizing the initiation cues and establishing two-on-one control. No escape attempts - focus entirely on identifying the choking arm advancement and locking it down at chest level. Start at 20% resistance and gradually increase.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 2: Chin Defense and Barrier Creation
training_progressions.focus: Building the secondary defensive layer of chin tucking and shoulder elevation
training_progressions.description: Partner has harness and actively works to advance the choking arm at moderate resistance. Defender uses two-on-one grip plus chin tuck and shoulder elevation as combined defense. Partner varies attack angles to test the chin defense from different entry points. Defender practices maintaining both grip defense and chin protection simultaneously.

training_progressions.focus: Executing the full escape from harness defense through guard recovery
training_progressions.description: Partner has harness with at least one hook and attacks with the choke at 70% resistance. Defender works the complete sequence: control choking arm, protect neck, strip one hook, hip escape, turn toward underhook, and recover to guard. Reset if choke is locked. Focus on smooth transitions between defensive stages rather than explosive movements.

training_progressions.focus: Applying all defensive skills under full resistance with competition-level intensity
training_progressions.description: Positional sparring starting from full harness with both hooks. Attacker works submissions at full intensity while defender applies all defensive tools. Rounds last until escape or submission. Track escape success rate and identify which stage of defense breaks down most frequently for targeted drilling.
